    Submission to TCS 2004 Track 2: Logic, Semantics, Speciﬁcation and Veriﬁcation

    title. Implementing a bisimulation-checker in FreshOCaml

    author. Murdoch J. Gabbay

    aﬃl. LIX email. gabbay@lix.polytechnique.fr

    tel. fax. addr. Laboratoire d’Informatique (LIX), École Polytechnique,

    91128 Palaiseau Cedex, France.

    author. Lucian Wischik aﬃl. Microsoft Corporation

    email. lu@wischik.com

    Abstract. We have implemented several diﬀerent formalisms of the pi calculus and its late bisimulation. Unexpectedly, even very diﬀerent formalisms turned out to have almost identical code—notably the original due to Milner, one based on FM-theory due to Gabbay, and one based on Higher-Order Abstract Syntax due to Miller and Tiu.

    Implementing a bisimulation-checker in FreshML

    Murdoch J. Gabbay (INRIA) Laboratoire d’Informatique (LIX), École Polytechnique

    91128 Palaiseau Cedex - France gabbay@lix.polytechnique.fr

    Lucian Wischik Microsoft Corporation

    lu@wischik.com

    1 Introduction

    In codice, veritas. There have been numerous diﬀerent ‘mathematical’ presentations of the pi-calculus and its theory of bisimulation (e.g. [2, 5, 6, 9]). Our intuition was that one particular presentation, that of Gabbay [2] was better than the others—cleaner and simpler. To demonstrate this we turned several presentations into actual implementations. Our intuition turned out false: despite its unconventional mathematical foundation Gabbay’s yielded code which was little diﬀerent from the others.

    Our implementations eﬀectively constitute half of a model-checker: the code for terms in the pi-calculus (i.e. states), and for labelled transitions between terms, and for checking whether the transitions out of one term match those out of another. These are precisely the areas that one ﬁnds in a mathematical presentation of the pi-calculus. The other half of the model checker, which we have not implemented, involves generating a graph of transitions and collapsing the duplicate states. We have been purposefully naïve in our code—it stays close to the spirit and the letter of the original mathematical formalisms.

    It is worth noting that the bisimulation checker in this paper are very simple. Each ﬁts on a single page of A4, albeit in a small font size. Implementing a bisimulation-checker for pi might be considered as a standard undergraduate exercise, alongside implementing a combinator machine for the lambda-calculus.

    Methodologically, one must ask whether implementing a formalism is a valid approach, and whether it has signiﬁcance. For validity, our idea was that a formalism’s mathematical clarity should be reﬂected in the clarity of its code; its formality shoudl be reﬂected in how close its code is to its maths; its abstractness should be reﬂected in how modular the code is. For signiﬁcance, we found that the implementations gave us a deeper understanding of pi-calculus semantics in a way which theory alone did not. This paper attempts to share that understanding. In particular we wish to communicate our excitement at the unexpected result—that the diﬀrerences in theory turned out at the programming level. In eﬀect, the implementations are a denotation for the formalisms!

    We remark on our implementation of Miller and Tiu’s presentation of the pi-calculus [5]. They deﬁne pi-calculus transitions and bisimulation in a particular form of logic, Higher-Order Abstract Syntax (HOAS). Because of this, bisimulation statements can be veriﬁed with a theorem-prover for that logic. We came to understand the logic’s primitives as an Application Programming Interface (API) layer between the pi-calculus and a theorem-prover. When we implemented the primitives using tuples, the resulting program was more-or-less the same as our other implementation. When we implemented them using features provided by our functional language (FreshOCaml [1]) the resulting program was somewhat diﬀerent.

    Source folio I

    Background

    The pi-calculus was introduced by Milner, Parrow, and Walker in [6], in 1992. Its operational semantics are described through a labelled transition system—the labelled transition means ‘a term can perform the action , so evolving to . The action may be the emission of data, the reception of data, or an internal move (called ).

    The pi-calculus uses a notion of behavioural equivalence called a bisimulation relation—for and to be bisimilar then any must be matched by a such that and are themselves bisimilar.

    These simple-looking deﬁnitions are subtle notably because of fresh names: when emits a freshly generated name then should be able to emit any other freshly generated name rather than speciﬁcally the same one; however when receives data then should be able to receive that same data. The various alternative presentations of the pi-calculus stem largely from attempts to make these matters more clear, more formal, or more abstract.

    Plan of paper.

    Section 2 gives the original pi-calculus semantics, and a direct implementation of in in the OCaml language. We remark that some eﬀort is needed o account for bound names, alpha-renaming and capture-avoiding substitution. To avoid this eﬀort in the rest of the paper we then switch to Fresh OCaml, whose built-in features provide a more elegant treatment of bound names. Section 3 considers what happens if we drop bound output transitions and use FM binding implement them instead, as discussed in [2]. The subsequent sections cover alternative semantics of Sewell and Miller/Tiu.

    FreshOCaml

    We have also implemented the same pi calculus in FreshOCaml (Figure 2). FreshOCaml is a conservative extension of OCaml which adds bindable types. These simplify the implementation of calculi with bound names. The practical eﬀect is to simplify the implementation of substitution (the function subs) and clash-avoidance (the function ). We give here a brief practical tutorial on FreshOCaml; for more information, see [1, 10].

    The following declares that ‘atom’ is a bindable type:

    type atom=unit name;;

    (Bindable types are piggy-backed onto a base type, in this case ‘unit’. It is done this way because piggy-backed types are easy to add to OCaml. The base type is not important, and indeed is not present in FreshML). A bindable type behaves much like unit ref in ML. The underlying implementation of a:atom is (say) an integer. Programs evolve in a global state containing an integer counter; each time a fresh name generated the value of the counter is used to implement it, and the counter is incremented. The following expression will inject a fresh name into the state:

    let n=(fresh:atom) in ...

    The signiﬁcant diﬀerence from unit ref is that the declaration of atom also introduces a polymorphic swapping function:

    swap : atom -> atom -> ’X -> ’X

    The literal operational meaning of swap a and b in t in the compiler is to swap a and b in the underlying representation of t. (If ’X is a complex data object, the swapping might be implemented lazily for eﬃciency.)

    When a bindable-type ‘atom’ is declared, FreshOCaml also generates a type-constructor <<atom>>’X for abstractions of atom. The abstraction is implemented internally as a pair (a,t). However, it can only be pattern-matched by concreting it, as for example in the ‘unpacking’ below:

    let unpack = function <<a>>t -> (a,t);;

    This works as follows. When matching an abstraction whose internal implementation is (n,exp), against this pattern , the compiler generates a fresh atom m and binds m to a and t to swap m n exp. Thus unpack <<a>>>t evaluates to (m,swap m n t) for some fresh m.

    Abstractions and concretions make it easier to work with fresh and bound names. This is particularly evident in the code for function subs in Figure 2, which we describe mathematically now. Substitution on atoms is as normal: if and otherwise. Substitution on terms is as below. Capture-avoidance comes for free: there is no need to explicitly generate a fresh name in the bound-input or restriction case, since a fresh name is implicitly generated by concreting. (Quantiﬁers, when omitted, are universal and outermost. The quantiﬁer is pronounced ‘for fresh ’ and mathematically means for all but ﬁnitely many (this provides a ‘context-free’ notion of ‘fresh for’, since any context, if it is of syntax or syntax-like objects, will only mention ﬁnitely many names [3, 10]).

    The two programs correspond line-for-line. ref () in the ﬁrst corresponds to fresh in the second (we may specify fresh:atom but the interpreter would infer that anyway). We use colour highlighting. So we see that we have exploited some ML state to generate fresh names. The only signiﬁcant diﬀerence is that in the ﬁrst version we often have to explicitly freshen bound names; the clauses Rcv and New in subs, Ebsnd and Ercv in , , and , and the (Ercv,Ercv) clause of .

    Unfortunately FreshOCaml does not allow non-linear patterns over names, which means that the pattern for choosing the same bound name for a pair of abstractions, is not possible. This is why renamings still appear for example in the Ebsnd clause of and the (Ercv,Ercv) clause of .

    Sometimes we use swap in the FreshOCaml version. For a name which we have just generated fresh, swapping and substitution are equivalent. However, swapping is probably more eﬃcient in FreshOCaml because ﬁrstly it is primitive (and not deﬁned, e.g. by induction on particular types) and second swappings are distributed into the calculation lazily while substitutions are evaluated call-by-value according to the standard ML evaluation strategy.

    Some of this is not necessary in the FreshOCaml version becuase in pattern-matching the compiler chooses fresh names. , for example, comes out signiﬁcantly cleaner.

    Note also that and appear earlier in the OCaml version: they are simply needed earlier for renamings in . We could ﬁx that by taking advantage of ML’s global state and generating unit ref as needed.

    A problem with FreshOCaml is that because there is no canonical ordering on names, it is hard to write eﬃcient lookup functions on tables indexed by names. These and other problems are being worked on in Cambridge now; for our purposes we simply note that delegating -equivalence to FreshOCaml makes our programs a little cleaner so we take advantage of this in future.

    5 Pi calculus in HOAS

    Miller and Tiu’s implementation of the pi-calculus is based on a new logic with a -quantiﬁer built-in, which creates a fresh name. Renaming is also built-in; function types and -reduction. For the case of -reduction for a fresh name generated by , the reduction is what Miller calls a -reduction, which can be thought of as a renaming of a name for a fresh name.

    We believe -reduction is susceptible to an FM-style semantics. This is for other, future, work.     In this program abstractions are function types atom->proc. Most of the time (see below) we achieve substitution with function application to a fresh name (-reduction, we generally call them m) or to a possibly not fresh name (-reduction, on variables, we generally call them n). As the reader probably knows it is up to us to program substitution into every process: the term New(function a -> if a=b then P1 else P2) is an exotic term, not corresponding to a textual substitution. subs is useful to build these processes; see the second line of the brief demonstration (in blue, though admittedly substituting in Nil is no great challenge; but because we have subs, see the trick discussed below, any p’ is admissible and even a variable of type proc).

    We still use fresh to generate fresh names in subs and . We also use an interesting FreshOCaml trick in the clauses for Rcv and New in subs, without which it would be hard to implement subs at all: we use swaps to rename atoms m and a in a function f, to avoid name-clash. Without the FM dynamic duo of name-generation fresh and name-swapping swap, this would be harder to express.

    We must now ask why we deﬁne subs if we have functions and application as discussed above. We need it in because we interpret (Open) very literally in by applying f to m.

    Miller and Tiu use Logic Programming; the logic of Generic Judgements (or logics derived from it) is intended to be implemented directly as a logic programming language, so that the mathematical speciﬁcation given [5] is the program.

    Thus our implementation misrepresents Miller and Tiu’s work by implementing it in a functional programming language. One could argue that Generic Judgements might well be implemented in some functional language, so that the programs we see are a fair reﬂection of the actual computation—but we must also remember that proof-search in a logic-programming language can be more ‘intelligent’ than that. For example, in the presence of matching [] a logical system might immediately add into the context where a functional implementation might systematically check all possibilities of and .

    6 Evaluation and related work

    The goal of this paper is to compare mathematical formalisms of the pi calculus, by implementing them. Our implementations mainly use FreshOCaml, an extension of OCaml based on FM theory and the ‘fresh’ operator [10]. We now explain the background for this choice of language.

    All implementations require fresh names, and generate them for the same reasons: for capture-avoiding substitution e.g. ()(); for clash-avoidance in the LTS rules par, com and res; and for comparing one bound transition with another in bisimulation.

    To implement fresh name generation, we ﬁrst used OCaml references, as in let n=ref(). Next we used FreshOCaml abstractions let n=(fresh:atom) and implicitly in pattern-matching . Both solutions amount to keeping a global state and deducing from it a free name. We could instead have implemented this global state ‘manually’, perhaps with a lazy free list or a counter, passed it explicitly to each function.

    Another possibility is to generate fresh names locally with respect to the processes in question, rather than globally. In eﬀect, we implement (() ) rather than ( fresh).

    Sewell’s version is close to the suggestions above: the explicit state of known names makes it easy to choose a fresh one.

    We are not proud of any of our solutions to the above issues. FreshOCaml seemed the least bad solution. Although it involves a global state, this global state at least has an elegant local mathematical treatment through the fresh operator [10]. The FreshOCaml implementation of substitution (the function subs in Figure 2) may be unfamiliar to most programmers, but it is more concise than the OCaml version (Figure 1).

    This paper only provides half a model-checker – the half to do with states and transitions. It does not deal with an entire transition graph, nor with collapsing equivalent states. This makes it unsuitable for terms with replication, and wildly ineﬃcient for weak bisimulation (which we therefore did not implement). For collapsing techniques speciﬁc to the pi calculus, see [8]. On the topic of collapsing states, we also mention History-Dependent Automata and HAL [11]. HD-automata use de-Bruijn notation; they represent the emission of a bound name by inserting a new index number 1 and shifting all the others along. We had hoped to implement HD-automata in the current paper, perhaps even in FM. However this turned out to miss the point. The chief contribution of HD-automata is its collapse of equivalent states.

    The established model-checker for the pi calculus is the Mobility Workbench [12]. One of its features is its use of symbolic bisimulation [4, 7] rather than the late bisimulation used in this paper. Symbolic bisimulation avoids substitution over all free names, and instead considers only substitutions that may aﬀect behaviour. We see our current work as complementary to the Mobility Workbench. So would pi model-checkers be better if they use a diﬀerent formalism for the pi calculus? No, all the formalisms yielded more or less the same code.
